explain.say: After the Moon, Venus is often the brightest thing in the night sky. It is the closest planet to Earth, and it is wrapped in thick white clouds that reflect most of the sunlight hitting them.

explain.say: Venus orbits closer to the Sun than we do, so from Earth it never strays far from the Sun in the sky. When it is to the east of the Sun, it shines in the west after sunset: the evening star.

faq.q: Why is Venus called the evening star?
faq.a: Because it often appears as a brilliant point in the west just after sunset, before any real stars come out. It isn't a star, though; it is a planet shining with reflected sunlight.
asks: Is the evening star a star?

faq.q: Why does Venus disappear for a while?
faq.a: Twice in each 584-day cycle it lines up with the Sun as seen from Earth, once passing in front and once going behind. Then it is lost in the Sun's glare, for days when in front and for weeks when behind.

faq.q: Why can't you see Venus at midnight?
faq.a: Venus orbits inside Earth's orbit, so from Earth it always appears fairly close to the Sun, never more than about 47 degrees away. It is seen in the evening or the morning, never high in the middle of the night.
asks: Why is Venus only seen near sunrise or sunset?

faq.a: It is the closest planet to Earth, it is fairly near the Sun, and it is covered in thick clouds that reflect about three quarters of the sunlight hitting them. Only the Sun and the Moon outshine it.

faq.q: Does Venus have phases like the Moon?
faq.a: Yes. Through a telescope Venus shows phases, from a thin crescent to nearly full. Galileo saw them in 1610, and they helped show that Venus orbits the Sun, not the Earth.
asks: Who discovered the phases of Venus?

facts: Venus overtakes Earth every 584 days, its cycle from evening star to morning star and back.
Venus's clouds reflect about three quarters of the sunlight that hits them.
Galileo observed the phases of Venus in 1610.
